questions.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+xy+2x+y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,-1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+xy+2x+y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+xy+2x+y)\text{ }j \\  & =(2x+y+2)\text{ }i+(-2y+x+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(1,-1) & =(2(1)+(-1)+2)\text{ }i+(-2(-1)+1+1)\text{ }j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,-1)}{‖∇f(1,-1)‖} & =\frac{3\,i+4\,j}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $2y-x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}).$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{2y}+1)i+(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{2{y}^{2}})-2)j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{y}-2)j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(\frac{1}{2}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{1}-2)j \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x-2) & =\frac{3}{2}(y-1) \\ -6(x-2) & =3(y-1) \\ -2(x-2) & =y-1 \\ -2x+4 & =y-1 \\ 2x+y-5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y) & ={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})j \\  & =(2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-2x)i+({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)+2y)j \\ ∇f(1,0) & =(2(1)(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(({1}^{2})(0))-2(1))i+((1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(({1}^{2})(0))+2(0))j \\  & =-2\,i+j \\  & =⟨-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,0)=⟨-2,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{-2} & =\frac{y-0}{1} \\ x-1 & =-2y \\ x+2y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{e}^{xyz}+{y}^{2},$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-2,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{e}^{xyz}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{e}^{xyz}+{y}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}{e}^{xyz}+{y}^{2})\,k \\  & =(2x+{x}^{2}yz){e}^{xyz}\,i+({x}^{3}z{e}^{xyz}+2y)\,j+{x}^{3}y{e}^{xyz}\,k \\ ∇f(1,-2,0) & =(2(1)+({1}^{2})(-2)(0)){e}^{1(-2)(0)}\,i+(({1}^{3})(0){e}^{1(-2)(0)}+2(-2))\,j+({1}^{3})(-2){e}^{1(-2)(0)}\,k \\  & =2\,i-4\,j-2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $2\,i-4\,j-2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=3$ at the point $(-1,-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=3.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,-1,1) & =2(-1)\text{ }i+2(-1)\text{ }j+2(1)\text{ }k \\  & =-2\,i-2\,j+2\,k \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{-2}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ x+1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz$ at the point $(1,0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

questions.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}=1$ at the point $(0,0,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, note that we can write the equation of our surface as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,0,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,0,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+\frac{2y}{9}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{2}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,0,2) & =2(0)\text{ }i+\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }j+\frac{(2)}{2}\text{ }k \\  & =k \\  & =⟨0,0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the vector form of the equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(0,0,2)$ and passes through the point $(0,0,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨0,\,0,\,2⟩+t\,∇f(0,0,2)=⟨0,\,0,\,2⟩+t\,⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)k \\  & =(2xy{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-2xz)i+({x}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-1)j+(2z\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2})k \\ ∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =(2(-1)(\frac{\pi }{2})(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-2(-1)(1))i+((-1)^{2}(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-1)j+(2(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-(-1)^{2})k \\  & =(-\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+2)i+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-1)j+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-1)k \\  & =2\,i-j+k \\  & =⟨2,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ and passes through the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1⟩+t\,∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)=⟨-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1⟩+t\,⟨2,-1,1⟩,\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y) = x^2 + 2y^2 +x$ that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1, 1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,1).$  

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,j \\  & =(2x+0+1)\,i+(0+4y+0)\,j \\  & =(2x+1)\,i+4y\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(2(1)+1)\,i+4(1)\,j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we want a unit normal vector, we normalize $\nabla f(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,1)}{‖∇f(1,1)‖} & =\frac{3\,i+4\,j}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the plane curve $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0, 4).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16} - 1,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(0,4).$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)j \\  & =\frac{2x}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{8}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{(4)}{8}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j \\  & =⟨0,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{x-{x}_{0}}=\frac{{v}_{y}}{{v}_{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{y}(x-{x}_{0}) & ={v}_{x}(y-{y}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(x-0) & =0(y-4) \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that the equation of the normal line to the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1$ at the point $(0,4)$ is $x=0.$

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z) = \ln (x^2 - xy) - z,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2){:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)k \\  & =(\frac{2x-y}{{x}^{2}-xy})\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{y-x})\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =(\frac{2\cdot 2-1}{{2}^{2}-2\cdot 1})\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{1-2})\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{3}{2}i-\,j-k \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf v = \langle v_x, v_y, v_z \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2)= \left\langle  \dfrac {3} {2}, -1, -1\right  \rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})}=\frac{y-1}{-1}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-1} \\ \frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

*$\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $C$ that passes through the point $P.$ *

This property is one of the most important facts in multivariable calculus since it gives a fundamental  link between
calculus and geometry!

Let's illustrate this property with a concrete example. Consider the paraboloid $z = f (x, y)=  x^2 + y^2$ and the level curve $\color{red}C$ of $f(x,y)$ corresponding to the point $P(1,-1).$  It is easy to see that  $\color{red}C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ with equation $x^2+y^2 = 2.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14252852/assets/f2461dbfcde2403e6ed7de9d6288d33a4deb52319d35b7036628c3fa8b3789dc.png)

In this particular instance, the property says that

*$\nabla \! f(1,-1)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $\color{red}C$ that passes through the point $P(1,-1).$ *

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14252852/assets/481b68af522b9144e232d9c775f734cd998b31a21571cbfd983c23d0f68c3688.png)

Looking at the situation in the $xy$-plane, we see the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14252852/assets/ceb353d5164d6aa089a37e77c9469d747ef4430e363e42f9d35ee6d769d9a4e4.png)

Let's verify that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is a normal line to the level curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-1).$

- First, computing the gradient, we find that $\nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle.$ Therefore, 

$$
\nabla f(1,-1) = \langle 2, -2 \rangle.
$$

- Then, using elementary calculus, we can show that the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$ is $y=x-2.$ Since this line has slope $m=1,$ it follows that the vector $\langle 1,1 \rangle$  is parallel to the level curve.

- Finally, taking the dot product between the gradient and the tangent vector, we obtain

$$
\nabla f(1,-1)\cdot  \langle 1,1 \rangle = \langle 2, -2\rangle \cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = 0.
$$

This means that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is *perpendicular* to the tangent line to $C$ at $(1,-1).$

tutorials.name: The Gradient as a Normal Vector For Functions of More than Two Variables
tutorials.problem:
The same property holds true in the case of three or more variables. In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if  the  gradient vector is nonzero, i.e., 

$$
\nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0,
$$

then we have the following result:

*$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $f(x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_n) =f(\mathbf y)$ at $\mathbf y.$*

To illustrate, let's consider the function  

$$
w = f (x, y, z)= \dfrac 1 2\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2-1\right).
$$

 

The level surface corresponding to $w=0$ is the sphere $\mathcal S$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 +z^2 =1.$ 

The point $P(0,0,1)$ lies on $\mathcal S.$ Computing $\nabla f(0,0,1),$ we get

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla f(x,y,z) &= \langle f_x, \: f_y, \:f_z\rangle \[5pt]
&= \dfrac12\langle2x, \: 2y, \: 2z\rangle\[5pt]
&= \langle x, \: y, \: z\rangle\[10pt]

\nabla f(0,0,1) &= \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1 \rangle.
}
$$

Now clearly, $\nabla f (0,0, 1)$ is perpendicular to $\mathcal S$ at the point $(0,0,1).$
